subject: Non-linear regression in a beta-binomial problem

messages.author: b1e64236b865525c
messages.subject: Non-linear regression in a beta-binomial problem
parts:
I'm not super familiar with Stan, so perhaps I shouldn't be messing with multilevel modeling, but well...

I'd like to model the probability of success of a binary event using a direct parametrization, instead of, say, modeling the log-odds. That probability declines over time: when days = 0, there's a fairly high success probability (say ~50%), and but it tends to an asymptotic, lower value (say ~5%). So I guess I have to use at least three parameters: initial (p when days = 0), asymptote and what I've called scale (in my formulation, lower values of scale amount to faster convergence to the asymptote). All three parameters may vary among groups, so I'm trying to use partial pooling with a hierarchical model.

When trying to fit the model below, things get really slow, and I get so many error messages, and of so many different kinds, that I come to think it must be severely misspecified. Is there any obvious way in which my code is wrong? By the way, I'm trying to describe my beta distributions using phi and kappa in much the same way as Carpenter 2016.

(*) theta = asymptote + scale * (initial - asymptote) / (scale + days), theta being the success probability.


data {
    int <lower = 1> N_group_days;
    int <lower = 1> N_group;
    int <lower = 1, upper = N_group> group [N_group_days];
    int <lower = 0> days [N_group_days];
    int <lower = 0> success [N_group_days];
    int <lower = 1> total [N_group_days];
}

parameters {
    vector <lower = 0, upper = 1> [N_group] initial;
    vector <lower = 0, upper = 1> [N_group] asymptote;
    vector <lower = 0> [N_group] scale;
    real <lower = 0> scale_lower;
    real <lower = 0> scale_delta;
    real <lower = 0, upper = 1> initial_phi;
    real <lower = 0> initial_kappa;
    real <lower = 0, upper = 1> asymptote_phi;
    real <lower = 0> asymptote_kappa;
}

transformed parameters {
    vector <lower = 0, upper = 1> [N_group_days] theta;
    real <lower = 0> scale_upper;
    for (i in 1: N_group_days) theta [i] = asymptote [group [i]] + scale [group [i]] * (initial [group [i]] - asymptote [group [i]]) / (scale [group [i]] + days [i]);
    scale_upper = scale_lower + scale_delta;
}

model {
    success ~ binomial (total, theta);
    initial ~ beta (initial_phi * initial_kappa, (1 - initial_phi) * initial_kappa);
    initial_phi ~ uniform (0, 1);
    initial_kappa ~ pareto (1, 1.15);
    
    asymptote ~ beta (asymptote_phi * asymptote_kappa, (1 - asymptote_phi) * asymptote_kappa);
    asymptote_phi ~ uniform (0, 1);
    asymptote_kappa ~ pareto (1, 1.15);
    
    scale ~ uniform (scale_lower, scale_upper);
    scale_lower ~ uniform (0, 20);
    scale_delta ~ uniform (0, 20);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Non-linear regression in a beta-binomial problem
parts: You can't declare a parameter like this:

because there are parameter values that satisfy the constraint
(lower = 0) that do not have support in that uniform distribution.
You need to declare:

vector<lower=scale_lower, upper=scale_lower + scale_delta> scale;

There may be other issues with the model, but that's a biggy.

I used pareto(..., 1.5) as that corresponded to the uniform on
the log prior count or something like that (got it out of Gelman et
al's Bayesian Data Analysis, chapter 5).

Our advice is always to try simpler models first and add complexity
a step at a time to isolate where problems arise.

We don't generally recommend these hard constraints, even with sliding
boundaries. You wind up putting strange distributions on the actual
values you care about (here scale) and things are very hard to identify.
If you have a lower value and upper value, the bounds want to be close
to those values to optimize likelihood, which can lead to sending the
unconstrained values out to extreme values.

- Bob

parts:
Thanks a lot, Bob!
But...
1. After all should I use vector <lower=scale_lower, upper=scale_lower + scale_delta> [N_group] scale or should I simply use vector [N_group] scale? I'm thinking of removing that scale_lower/delta/upper thing altogether and just putting a single prior on scale...
2. About trying simpler models first and add complexity a step at a time: does that mean I try to fit a model using the data of one particular group, then try a hierarchical model? Not sure if that would help...? And after I replicated what you did in your (excellent) case study, I tried to do something similar (i.e. a multilevel model) to predict whether or not the Golden State Warriors will have at least 74 wins this season, and got some seemingly solid results.
Thanks again.

> scale ~ uniform (scale_lower, scale_upper);

(lower = 0) that do not have support in that uniform distribution.

There may be other issues with the model, but that's a biggy.

the log prior count or something like that (got it out of Gelman et
al's Bayesian Data Analysis, chapter 5).

Our advice is always to try simpler models first and add complexity
a step at a time to isolate where problems arise.  

We don't generally recommend these hard constraints, even with sliding
boundaries.  You wind up putting strange distributions on the actual
values you care about (here scale) and things are very hard to identify.
If you have a lower value and upper value, the bounds want to be close
to those values to optimize likelihood, which can lead to sending the
unconstrained values out to extreme values.  

- Bob

parts:
You need to define the log density in such a way that it
is always finite for parameter values that meet all the declared
constraints.

Yes, start with simpler models where fewer things vary and then
make them more complicated. It's not always easy to stage a model
that way.

- Bob
